data.name: Don't Get Hit In The Face
data.detailed_description:
Don't Get Hit In The face is a movement-based active virtual reality game. Do whatever you need to do... duck, weave, dodge and crawl... just don't get hit in the face! Taking gameplay influences from old-school arcade games and combining that with room-scale VR, DGHITF is as simple as it sounds, and that's what makes it fun.

Don't Get Hit In The Face includes 4 game modes of increasing difficulty, and an awesome 13 song soundtrack. It's fun on its own as VR arcade game, and is also an excellent addition to a VR workout regimen.

reviews.review:
Don't Get Hit In The Face is a straightforward virtual reality arcade experience that turns one basic instruction into its entire gameplay philosophy: keep your head away from everything flying toward it. Developed and published by DracoSoftware, LLC, the game avoids complicated controls and instead relies heavily on physical movement. Players must duck, lean, crouch, and shift their bodies to escape incoming obstacles. The result is an uncomplicated but energetic VR experience that demonstrates how entertaining a single mechanic can become when the player's own movement is effectively the controller.

The gameplay is designed specifically around room-scale virtual reality. Rather than pressing a button to perform a dodge, players physically move themselves out of danger. Obstacles approach from different positions, forcing quick reactions and an awareness of the available play space. Early challenges are easy enough to understand almost immediately, but the difficulty gradually places greater demands on timing and reflexes. Because successful play requires frequent movement, sessions can become surprisingly physical. It is easy to begin casually and discover several minutes later that the game has effectively turned into a light workout.

Four different game modes provide increasing difficulty levels and give players a reason to continue improving after learning the fundamentals. The underlying concept remains largely unchanged, but tougher challenges demand faster responses and more precise movement. Leaderboard support complements the arcade structure particularly well, encouraging players to chase higher scores rather than expecting traditional campaign progression. Four Steam achievements offer another small collection of goals. These features cannot completely eliminate repetition, but they provide useful incentives for anyone who enjoys mastering simple mechanics and improving personal performance.

Presentation is deliberately functional rather than extravagant. Visuals primarily exist to make approaching hazards easy to identify so that players have enough information to react. This clarity matters considerably in a game where hesitation can immediately end a successful run. A soundtrack containing 13 songs helps give the action additional energy and makes repeated attempts more enjoyable. The music fits naturally with the constant movement, giving the experience an almost rhythm-game quality at certain moments even though avoiding obstacles remains the central objective.

The largest weakness is the relatively narrow amount of content. This is not a VR adventure filled with exploration, storytelling, upgrades, characters, or extensive progression systems. Once players have experienced the available modes, continued enjoyment largely comes from chasing better scores and becoming more proficient at avoiding hazards. Anyone who enjoys arcade-style repetition may appreciate this focused approach, but players expecting substantial mechanical evolution could lose interest relatively quickly. The game works best in shorter sessions where its physical nature and immediate challenge remain entertaining instead of exhausting.

Its technical requirements are modest by modern standards. The game requires SteamVR and tracked controllers, with room-scale movement forming an essential part of the experience. Approximately 2 by 1.5 meters of available play space is recommended, so having a safe environment is arguably more important than having particularly powerful hardware. The minimum specifications include an Intel i3-class processor, 2 GB of RAM, and a GTX 970-class graphics card, while the recommended configuration moves toward an Intel i5, 4 GB of RAM, and a GTX 1060. Storage requirements are extremely small at roughly 120 MB.

Steam Deck compatibility is effectively not applicable as a conventional handheld experience because this is a VR-only game that depends on SteamVR, tracked motion controllers, and physical room-scale movement. It should not be considered a normal Steam Deck game that can simply be installed and played using the Deck's built-in screen and controls. Even if specialized configurations could theoretically involve a Steam Deck, the game's intended hardware and control setup makes a dedicated PC VR environment the practical way to experience it.

Don't Get Hit In The Face succeeds primarily through commitment to its uncomplicated idea. It does not pretend to offer enormous depth, and its limited variety will prevent it from satisfying players seeking a substantial VR campaign. What it does provide is an accessible, energetic arcade challenge where reflexes and genuine physical movement matter more than memorizing complex controls. The combination of increasingly difficult modes, leaderboards, achievements, music, and naturally active gameplay makes it particularly suitable for short VR sessions and score chasing. Its simplicity is simultaneously its greatest strength and its biggest limitation, but for players who appreciate physically demanding VR arcade games, there is genuine entertainment in trying to follow the game's most important rule.

Rating: 6/10
